problem_html:
H-JEPA plans top-down. A level-2 world model, optimised by gradient descent over 800 candidate latent-action sequences, proposes the next latent subgoal. A level-1 model-predictive controller (MPC) then tries to reach that subgoal within 10 environment steps before the whole hierarchy replans. Nothing in this loop checks whether the subgoal is actually executable by the low-level controller under its horizon and search budget.

RASR adds three pieces on top of the frozen, pretrained H-JEPA:

  1. Reachability estimator R(zt, g, H, B): probability that the level-1 MPC with budget B reaches latent subgoal g from the current latent zt within H steps, trained on real MPC executions.
  2. Reachability-aware selection (P2): rerank the unchanged level-2 candidate pool by progress cost − λ·cmin·log(R + δ).
  3. Failure monitoring + local repair (P3): detect stalls from planner-visible signals, re-solve the subgoal with a reachability term (and a visited-region penalty), and fall back to full replanning when the repaired subgoal is still unreachable.

Research question: under the same evaluation tasks and comparable compute, does reachability + local repair beat plain H-JEPA, more frequent replanning, and full replanning on the same trigger?
mermaid:
flowchart TB
  O[current frame o_t] --> E[frozen H-JEPA encoders]
  G[goal frame] --> E
  E --> L2[level-2 GD planner 800 candidates]
  L2 -->|candidate subgoals + progress cost| P2[P2 rerank cost - λ log R]
  R[(reachability MLP R z,g,H,B)] --> P2
  P2 -->|subgoal g| L1[level-1 MPC 100 samples, 10 steps]
  L1 --> ENV[FourRoom env]
  ENV --> O
  ENV -.-> M{monitor subgoal misses / goal stall}
  M -->|trigger| RP[P3 repair GD with R + novelty terms]
  R --> RP
  RP -->|R below tau| FB[fallback: full replan]
  RP --> L1
  FB --> L1
setup_html:
• Code: official kevinghst/H-JEPA at commit 97054ec, unmodified. All RASR code wraps or subclasses upstream objects; with every RASR switch off the planner is bit-identical to upstream (regression test).
  • Environment: FourRoom Distractors (224×224 pixels, one moving distractor, agent speed 2.5 px/step, success = within 16 px of the goal, 210-step budget). Chosen as the first environment because it needs no MuJoCo rendering, has an env-native success signal and its state can be restored exactly for branching rollouts. Visual AntMaze and an offline DROID check were added afterwards with the same code (sections AntMaze and DROID).
  • Model / planner: pretrained 2-level H-JEPA (seed 42) with the official fourroom_l2 planner: level-2 GD with 800 samples and a decaying horizon of 12; level-1 GD MPC with 100 samples, a horizon of 2 × 5-step action blocks, replanning every 10 steps.
  • Tasks and splits: test = the official 50 start–goal tasks (two-room crossings). Train (40) and val (20) task sets were generated with the official generator under different seeds (1001, 2002 vs. 3072), so no start–goal configuration is shared. Train is used to fit the reachability models; every threshold, temperature and λ is chosen on val.
  • Determinism: upstream resets FourRoom without a seed, and two runs of the official eval.py gave different step counts (168 vs 141 on task 0). We seed each reset (100000 + task) and enable deterministic torch kernels; runs are bit-reproducible across processes.
  • Privileged state: simulator xy is used only for labels' calibration, evaluation and the analysis-only latent→xy probe in figures. The planner sees pixels, latents, model predictions and the reachability model.
  • Hardware: one RTX 4090 shared by up to 7 jobs. Wall-clock numbers are therefore inflated; predictor call counts are the comparable compute measure.
p0_html:
The instrumented runner mirrors the upstream chunked evaluation (one world per task, planner generators reseeded to seed + task) and logs, per planning call: the latents of the current frame and goal, the level-1 subgoal, all predicted level-1/level-2 plans, horizons, gradient-descent iterations, predictor forward calls and wall-clock. Per step it logs xy, distractors, actions and the real-frame latents, plus an env snapshot before every planning call.

The seed-42 baseline reaches 86% (43/50), inside the paper's 81.3 ± 6.7% range. All 7 failures occur in tasks with every door open (7 of 14 such tasks fail; 36 of 36 tasks with a closed door succeed).
p1_html:
Attempt. Restore the env at a baseline planning call, freeze the level-2 subgoal g the baseline gave its level-1 MPC, and run only the frozen level-1 MPC towards g for 30 steps with budget B ∈ {B0 = 2 GD iterations × 4 samples, B1 = 10 × 20, B2 = 90 × 100 (baseline)}. Labels for H ∈ {5, 10, 20, 30} are prefixes of the same rollout. Label: Y = 1 iff mink≤H ‖enc2(ot+k) − g‖² ≤ ε, with ε = 6.70: the median latent distance between real frames whose agents are within 8 px (about 3 agent steps), computed on the train split only.

A restored branch reproduces the logged frame to within 1/255 per pixel. Branch-B2 labels agree with the baseline's own execution of the same subgoal for 84% (H = 10) of 500 matched calls; the rest is solver noise, so labels are partly stochastic.
p1_after_html: The distance-only logistic model already reaches 0.877 AUROC: most of the reachability signal is "how far is the subgoal, and how much budget and time does the controller get". The MLP adds a clear gain within each (H, B) cell (0.853 vs 0.751 for kNN and 0.731 for the reference), and after temperature scaling on val it is the best-calibrated model (ECE 0.022). Three MLP training seeds give test AUROC 0.870, 0.906 and 0.903.

footer: All numbers on this page are generated from the experiment logs by scripts/build_site.py. FourRoom: model seed 42, planner seeds 42/43/44; AntMaze: model and planner seed 42; DROID: model seed 1 (baseline: 3 model seeds), planner seeds 1/2/3. See Limitations.
abstract: We reproduce hierarchical H-JEPA planning on FourRoom Distractors (86% success), learn a controller-conditioned reachability model for its latent subgoals (test AUROC 0.903, well calibrated), and use it for subgoal reranking and local repair. Over three planner seeds on the 50 official tasks, reachability-aware selection and repair score 84.7% against 85.3% for the baseline; the best variant is the repair without reachability (88.0%, not significant). Diagnosing why, we find the baseline's failures are not unreachable subgoals. The level-2 planner keeps choosing reachable subgoals that make no progress, a corner attractor that the world model scores as close to the goal. On Visual AntMaze, where failures are stalls, the repair without the reachability term is the only significant gain in the project (54.0% vs 38.0% over three planner seeds, +33 / −9 of 150 episodes, p < 0.001), while adding the reachability term hurts (26.7%, p = 0.01). On DROID (offline, open loop) reachability-aware selection has no effect with either label.
kpi_p23_label: RASR vs baseline success, mean over 3 planner seeds (150 episodes each); no significant change
p23_method_html:
Candidate pool (P2). After the unchanged level-2 GD solve, all 800 optimised candidates are rolled out once (one extra batched forward). Each candidate gives a progress cost (the planner's own objective) and a first predicted latent, the subgoal level 1 would receive. B3 picks argminc costc − λ·cmin·log(R(zt, gc, H = 10, B2) + 0.05). λ is relative to the call's best cost, so λ = 0.25 accepts a candidate up to 25% more costly per unit of −log R.

Monitor (P3). Planner-visible and debounced: a trigger fires after 3 consecutive missed subgoals (the real frame's latent is not within ε of the previous subgoal) or when the real latent goal distance has not improved by 5% in 5 calls. After a trigger the repair stays active for 3 calls, followed by a 1-call cooldown.

Repair (Ours). Re-run the level-2 GD with the cost augmented by −λR·cmin·log R(z, ĝ1) (differentiable through the frozen MLP) and +β·cmin·visit(ĝ1:2), a kernel penalty on plan waypoints near latents already observed in this episode. If the repaired subgoal still has R < 0.3, fall back to a plain full replan. B4 uses the same trigger but only re-solves (fresh restart, min cost). Ablation: the same repair with λR = 0 and no rerank. B2 replans every 5 instead of 10 steps (twice the planning calls). λ ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 1.0} and β ∈ {5, 20} were chosen on the val tasks; the test set was run once per method.

Before tuning anything on val, the first prototypes were tried on three failed test tasks (9, 16, 30). That is where the failure mode below was found. None of those prototypes solved them, and the configurations reported here were fixed on val.
p23_table_note: Δ: tasks gained and lost relative to B1 on the same 50 tasks, with an exact two-sided McNemar test. Recovery: share of triggers after which the real latent goal distance improves by ≥ 5% within 4 calls. L2 predictor calls include the extra pool rollouts and re-solves. Planning seconds were measured with 6–7 jobs sharing one GPU.
seeds_note: Planner seeds 43 and 44 re-run every method with the same model, tasks and env seeds. B2 (twice the planning calls, worst at seed 42) was run at seed 42 only to save compute. Pooled McNemar: exact test over the 150 (task, seed) pairs against B1 of the same seed. The paper's 81.3 ± 6.7% varies the model seed as well; ours varies the planner seed only.
p23_results_html:
Result over three seeds. Rerank (B3), full replanning (B4) and Ours all score 84.7% against 85.3 ± 1.8% for the baseline. The repair without reachability scores 88.0 ± 1.2% and is above the baseline at every seed, but the pooled difference (+5 / −1 tasks, p = 0.22) is not significant. At seed 42 alone, reranking changes 31% of subgoal choices (B3) without changing a single outcome. Ours loses task 45; the ablation without reachability gains task 33; B2 loses tasks 2 and 31 while doubling planner compute.

  • The reachability term makes repairs more conservative. Over the three seeds, the real goal distance improves after 70% of triggers without R, 47% with R, and 45% for plain full replanning. R favours short, safe subgoals, which helps when the subgoal is unexecutable and hurts when the problem is lack of progress.
  • False triggers cost time. The goal-stall trigger fires in 43 of 50 episodes, including most successful ones, because latent goal distance is not monotone even on good routes. Ours needs 180 steps per success vs 166 for B1 (3 seeds), and task 45 (solved by B1 in 179 steps) runs out of budget.
  • Compute. Ours adds about 4 level-2 re-solves per episode (+20% level-2 predictor calls); B2 doubles them (+108%). The MLP itself costs one batched forward per call.

p23_videos.cap: Task 33, repair without R: repairs fire at calls 3, 8 and 15 and the agent reaches the goal at step 168. This is the only task any method gained over the baseline.
Task 9, Ours: repairs fire at calls 6, 11 and 16 and produce subgoals rated reachable (R 0.54–0.76), but the episode still fails.
Task 45, Ours: a false trigger. The baseline solves this task in 179 steps; repeated conservative repairs slow the agent and it runs out of budget.

findings_html:
1. Baseline reproduced and made deterministic. 86% on the official tasks (paper 81.3 ± 6.7%). Upstream evaluation is not reproducible because env resets are unseeded; with seeded resets, runs are bit-identical.
  2. Subgoal reachability is predictable. Real MPC executions give balanced labels. An MLP on frozen latents plus (H, B) reaches 0.903 AUROC and 0.022 ECE on held-out tasks, and beats kNN and a distance-only model mainly within each controller condition. Low-level budget matters only at the extreme: 10 GD iterations × 20 samples (B1) reach subgoals as often as the default 90 × 100.
  3. Reachability correlates with failure but does not cause it here. Failed episodes reach 16% of their subgoals against 77% in successful ones. Inspecting them shows why: the level-2 planner keeps proposing subgoals in or near the start corner. They are often reachable, but the world model rates the corner as near-goal (level-2 cost ≈ 1.2–1.7 at the start of task 9). In some calls every one of the top-64 candidates has R ≈ 0.02. When the repair is pushed away from visited states, gradient descent returns off-manifold latents that the reachability model correctly scores as unreachable (R ≈ 0.02).
  4. Hence no success gain. Selecting or repairing by executability cannot fix a high-level model error about which subgoal makes progress. The one consistent positive signal (88.0% vs 85.3% over three seeds, not significant) comes from exploration pressure, the visited-region term without R, not from reachability. The predictor itself transfers reasonably to the candidates it scores (AUROC 0.85 on non-selected candidates), so the null result is not a predictor failure.
  5. AntMaze confirms the pattern with a significant result. Over three planner seeds, repair without R: 54.0% vs 38.0% (+33 / −9 of 150, p < 0.001), better than the baseline at every seed; full replan on the same trigger 48.0% (p = 0.01). With R the repair drops to 26.7%, below the baseline (p = 0.01). The val-selected predictor is close to a distance prior, so the R term pulls repaired subgoals back towards the stuck state and cancels the exploration term.
  6. DROID (offline): no effect with either the original or a time-aligned label (+0.5 points, p = 0.78). The original label mostly rewarded not moving.
limits_html:
• One model seed (the reachability model lives in its latent space) and three planner seeds; 150 episodes per method still leave pooled Wilson intervals of about ±6 points. B2 has one seed.
  • The reachability model was trained only on selected subgoals; on non-selected candidates its AUROC drops from 0.91 to 0.85 (measured on val tasks). Training on candidate attempts would close part of that gap.
  • Labels use a latent threshold calibrated on train real-frame pairs; an xy-probe label was not used.
  • The goal-stall trigger is noisy because latent goal distance is not a progress metric across walls. A better trigger (for example model-predicted vs realised progress) is likely the most useful fix.
  • A variant that bypasses the level-2 planner on a failed repair (level 1 aims at the real goal) was explored on 3 val tasks only, then dropped for compute.
  • Next: a progress-aware repair objective (for example route diversity across doors) and a better stall trigger. AntMaze and DROID results are in their own sections above; their limitations are listed there.
shift_intro_html: The predictor was trained only on subgoals the baseline selected, but reranking scores all 800 candidates. To measure the shift we replayed the 20 val episodes with logging only (bit-identical trajectory) and, at every second planning call, executed the baseline's subgoal plus four non-selected candidates spread over predicted R, from the same restored state with the B2 controller (1000 attempts).
shift_after_html: The MLP loses some accuracy off-distribution (AUROC 0.908 → 0.848, ECE 0.038 → 0.056), and kNN loses more (0.911 → 0.824). Among candidates of the same planning call, the MLP ranks a reached candidate above an unreached one 86% of the time (896 pairs, H = 10). So the reranker gets a meaningful signal, and the lack of a success gain is not explained by a broken predictor.
